The 2025 screening finding of partial alignment is a first assessment of that kind and does not show a change.

What remains is equal treatment of EU workers in the law on access to the labour market, including an end to posts in private companies reserved for nationals. The foreigners law is itself the barrier, the 2025 amendment only renames bodies and the further amendments are only proposed with unknown content (all statuses are proposals; the two government items are machine translated, so capped at Medium), while the country's general ban on nationality discrimination is its own account and does not close the gap. The Commission's statement that the law makes no EU distinction conflicts with the country's account on quotas, which is reported and partly explained under RI-FMW-002.

A key recommendation on non-discrimination against EU workers is repeated in the 2020 to 2025 reports, and equal access is central to the chapter. No benchmark or Reform Agenda payment condition under this issue was found in the evidence.

The change is legal and within the government's control, and the same law was amended in 2021 and 2025. Against that, six reports record no alignment and the requirement runs to the time of accession, so there is no evidence of past progress.

The chapter scale was not decisive, since this is part of the chapter and no sub-area wording matches; Commission items describe annual quotas and work permits unchanged from 2020 to 2025, and the 2025 seasonal work law leaves conditions for EU citizens to be specified. Permit counts (755 in 2021, some 8 900 in 2024) are not used as a trend, because the bases appear to differ: the 2021 figure sits beside 3 242 separate opinions in a machine-translated agency report, capped at Medium.

What remains is access for EU citizens without work permits or residence permits, with their explicit exclusion from quotas, and no responding intervention is linked (statuses are proposals). The confirmed contradiction stands: the Commission says the law does not distinguish EU citizens, while the country says quotas do not apply to them under a reciprocity agreement. Art. 5(2) point 1 of the 2015 law (machine translated, so capped at Medium, and used under LIM-0024) partly explains this, because it does exempt foreigners given equality under such an agreement, but it is conditional, no item identifies a concluded agreement or shows it applied, and the Commission still requires the exclusion.

Permits and quotas are central to the chapter, but they are named as requirements only in the 2024 report and the screening report, not in the annual key recommendation, which is why this is central with thin support. If the reviewers read the key recommendation on non-discrimination as covering permits and quotas, this would be High; the large item count is mostly the law's own text and did not count.

The change needs only national law, but it involves two laws and the interior and labour ministries and the Employment Agency, and an international organisation reports overlapping mandates between the laws. The law was amended in 2021 and 2025 without touching this requirement, and the proposed amendments have unknown content.

The chapter scale was not decisive, since this is part of the chapter and no sub-area wording matches. The finding that EU citizens cannot take public administration posts, apart from some in health and education, is unchanged in each report from 2020 to 2025.

What remains is limiting the restriction to posts involving public authority and the general interest of the State, in line with case law of the Court of Justice. No responding intervention is linked, so there is no status to compare, and the existing exemptions for health and higher education are the country's account and are narrower than the requirement.

This is a repeated finding central to the chapter, but public sector posts are named as a requirement only in the screening report and not in an annual key recommendation. If the reviewers read 'in all sectors' in the 2023 to 2025 key recommendation as covering them, this would be High.

The work is national and depends on no outside party, but it requires a careful review of civil servant categories across the public service against case law. There is no evidence of past progress and no responding intervention.

Sub-area wording on EURES, which matches this issue, says no developments or measures in 2020, 2021, 2022, 2024 and 2025, and the 2023 key recommendation still asks for alignment. The screening report's 'good level of preparation' sits in tension with these and with its own finding that no appointment system exists; it is the only rating of this kind, so I do not read it as improvement, and I report the tension rather than resolve it.

What remains is a legal system for appointing EURES members and partners and access for private employment agencies. The Commission credits good alignment on IT and structural levels, but every responding intervention is only proposed (these statuses are themselves proposals), with legislative amendments on a 2030 deadline and implementation at accession.

Alignment with EURES is named in the key recommendation in the 2023, 2024 and 2025 reports, and EURES is one of the chapter's main strands. The recommendation is a composite one, so the repetition is of one sentence and not of independent findings.

One lead body is planned and the IT and structural base is credited, which helps. However, no legal step has been reported in six years, the country's own timetable runs to 2030 and implementation is tied to accession.

The chapter scale was context only. The key recommendation to strengthen the Employment Service Agency is nearly unchanged in the 2023, 2024 and 2025 reports, which sets the default, and the 2025 report says the previous recommendations were not implemented. Training took place in 2023 and the screening report calls capacity satisfactory, but no earlier rating exists to show a rise from.

What remains is updated EURES training after staff turnover, with connection of private employment agencies and later ESCO mapping. The Commission finds the main IT elements in place and capacity satisfactory, and capacity building and IT upgrades are proposed here as implemented while further strengthening is only proposed; all these statuses are proposals.

Agency capacity is named in the key recommendation in three reports, so the requirement is repeated. It is not central now, because the Commission finds capacity satisfactory and the IT elements in place.

The remaining work rests mainly with one agency, does not depend on other countries and builds on training and IT delivered before. Past capacity building is reported by the Commission, not only by the government.

The chapter scale was context only. The composite recommendation naming the European Labour Authority is nearly unchanged in the 2023, 2024 and 2025 reports, and the only direct findings, in the screening report, say national law is not aligned.

What remains is aligning national law with the regulation and preparing the State Labour Inspectorate for coordinated tasks. Both responses are only proposed for the medium term, and the implemented training does not align the law; these statuses are proposals.

The authority is named in a key recommendation in three reports, but only as part of a sentence mainly about the employment service. The direct support is one source and the issue is not central to the chapter.

Harmonisation is within national control and plans exist, but the plans only run in the medium term, with full implementation at accession. They also need institutional and procedural preparation by the labour inspectorate as well as legal change.

The chapter scale was context only, and the issue's EU items come from one report, the 2025 screening report, so there is no sequence to read. The 2026 items are regional, concern migrant workers generally and cannot alone support a finding about the country.

What remains is designating an institution to support EU mobile workers and improving the system that informs them of their rights. No responding intervention is linked, so there is no status to compare.
The requirement appears in one report, in repeated sentences, and is not named in a key recommendation. The regional items do not raise this, as they concern other workers.

Designating an institution is a single national decision, with no dependence on others and few actors. There is no evidence of past progress, so this rests on the nature of the task and is less certain for the wider information system.

The chapter scale was context only, and the 2025 'good level of preparation' for coordination is a single rating with nothing before it. No new agreements are recorded in 2021, 2022, 2023, 2024 or 2025, despite negotiations started in 2023. Two confirmed count contradictions stand (14 against 13 EU agreements; 23 against 22 in total); they do not change this view and are not resolved here.

What remains is agreements with the other Member States and the administrative measures to prepare for accession. Agreements with 13 Member States are in force, by the government's own list and the Commission's count, but the negotiations with Italy and Greece are only proposed and no outcome is recorded; these statuses are proposals. Adopting further agreements would not by itself close the gap.

Concluding agreements is in the key recommendation in the 2021 to 2025 reports, and social security coordination is a main strand of the chapter. The Commission's good preparation rating lowers the urgency but not the repeated requirement, so reviewers may reasonably weigh centrality differently.
Progress depends on other states agreeing, not only on the government. No new agreement is recorded from 2021 to 2025, including after the negotiations started in 2023.

The chapter scale was context only, and the 2025 ratings have nothing earlier to compare with. The recommendation on administrative measures recurs from 2020 to 2025, and the shift from identifying measures to putting them in place reflects wording, not a reported step.

What remains is removing citizenship conditions from the pension and health insurance laws, aligning with the regulations and putting administrative measures in place by accession. The Commission finds the framework partly aligned, but the plan to amend the legislation is only proposed within five years (a status that is itself a proposal).

Administrative measures for coordination are in the key recommendation in each report from 2020 to 2025, and alignment with the regulations is central to this strand of the chapter. The screening report requires alignment, including on nationality conditions, by accession.

The named legal changes are within national control, and the register law adopted in 2023 shows some related legislative activity. However, it spans the pension and health systems, needs prior analysis and has a plan of up to five years.

The sub-area rating 'still at an early stage' matches this issue but appears only in the 2025 screening report, and the annual key recommendation adds electronic exchange only in 2025. The word 'still' suggests the issue is not new, so I do not call it new, and a single year cannot show a trend.

What remains is the human and IT capacity to exchange social security data through EESSI and to process EHIC data electronically. The registry and the EESSI preparations are only proposed (statuses that are themselves proposals), and the country reports no EHIC reader in its healthcare facilities.

Electronic exchange is central to applying coordination at accession, and the Commission asks for stepped-up effort. The support is thin, however, as it comes from the screening report and one annual key recommendation.

The planned registry has a stated World Bank loan and two-year horizon, but it rests on the country's own account. Several institutions are involved, EESSI access points follow later analysis over five years, and connection also involves the EU side, with no past progress recorded.

The chapter scale was context only. Nine agreements or nine Member States are recorded in each report from 2020 to 2024, and no development in 2024 and 2025. The 14 Member States in the 2025 report is a noted difference of scope, not growth, because the five added have agreements that do not include EHIC.

What remains is access through EHIC for citizens of the other Member States. Use with nine Member States is proposed as in practice (a status that is itself a proposal), and the Commission finds technical alignment satisfactory, but the card's use rests on separate arrangements and not on general entitlement.

This is a repeated finding across six reports, but the EHIC is not named in the key recommendation, which refers only to healthcare insurance agreements. The Commission treats technical alignment as satisfactory and it overlaps with RI-FMW-008.

The sources describe the basis differently: the country says unilateral use and the Commission says bilateral agreements, which matters because the first would be within national control and the second depends on others. The country reports that agreements could soon be reached with three more states, but no new agreement or development has been recorded.
All items come from one report, the 2025 screening report, so there is no sequence to read and the chapter scale cannot help.

What remains is alignment with Directives 98/49/EC and 2014/50/EU, apart from cross-border membership and equal treatment in voluntary funds. Those two exceptions are provided in law but enter into force only at accession, and no responding intervention is linked, so adoption does not count as closure.

The requirement is raised only in the screening report and in no key recommendation, and supplementary pensions are peripheral to the chapter compared with its main strands. It remains a stated acquis gap, so Low does not mean it can wait past accession.

Legal alignment is within national control and part of the framework is already drafted into law. However, the responsible unit is reported to have only one person and the Commission calls for thorough training.

The sub-area rating 'still at an early stage' matches this issue but appears only in 2025, so it is used with the issue's own items. The integrity policy is outstanding in 2023, 2024 and 2025, and the framework is called weak in 2024 and again in the screening report.

What remains is a signed integrity policy, a person to implement it, a reinforced internal audit department and controls in the institutions concerned. No responding intervention is linked, so there is no status to compare, and the country's stated plan to sign has not been shown to be carried out.

The requirement is repeated by the Commission in three reports, but it is not in a key recommendation for the chapter or central to it. The issue's scope is limited to free movement of workers, and general anti-corruption policy is outside it.

Signing the policy and naming a person are small steps for one agency, but no report shows them done, though the agency reportedly planned to do so. Reinforcing audit staff, ministry capacity and controls across institutions is wider.

The evidence is from international organisations, with one research study, and partly regional, and no measure of this issue repeats over time for the country. The doubling of permits is regional and cannot alone support a finding here, and the Commission's permit counts have unclear bases. The chapter scale was not decisive, as it concerns EU workers' access.

No EU requirement item exists for this issue, so the comparison the gap requires cannot be made and no responding intervention is linked. The international organisations report, for North Macedonia, regulatory barriers, passport retention, wage deductions, underreporting and overlapping laws, which is what remains on their account; other items are regional. A regional claim that laws are EU-aligned does not name the country and sits uneasily with the Commission's finding of partial alignment for EU workers.

The issue is mainly raised by others: the evidence is from international organisations and partly regional, with no Commission recommendation on third-country workers in Chapter 2. The labour shortage it describes may matter for the country, but that is not the test for importance to accession.

The rules and inspection are national matters, without dependence on the EU, but the international organisation evidence, partly regional, points to several institutions, under-resourced inspection and permits tied to one employer. No item shows past progress for the country, so this is a provisional view.

The Commission states that the 2019 amendments further simplified the single application, which is not government reporting alone, though no processing data supports it. The World Bank in 2024 still reports regulatory barriers and asks for simpler permits, and quotas are reported regionally to add delay, so the wider result is less clear.
The Commission directly ties the simplification to the amendments, but this is one statement in one report, with no before and after measure.

The Commission itself rates preparation on coordination as good and gives the experience of the agreements as the reason, so this is not government reporting alone. The result is narrow: it concerns readiness, and the same report still finds the law only partly aligned.
The Commission states the causal link directly, but 'including through' shows that it does not treat the agreements as the only source of this experience. No independent test of the link exists.

The Commission finds technical alignment satisfactory and says the agreements allow EHIC use, but only nine Member States are covered and the country reports that data cannot be processed electronically. The Commission asks for stepped-up capacity to be ready at accession.

The Commission says bilateral agreements allow the use, and the country lists agreements that include EHIC with nine Member States. However, the country also says use is on a unilateral basis, so the mechanism is not settled.
